Con vectores en la mano, la geometría se: With vectors in hand, geometry turns analytic: every figure becomes an equation, and drawing problems become calculations. A point plus a direction vector, which is what you learnt to handle in the previous topic, already describes a whole line. And the dot product equal to zero comes back as the test for perpendicularity.
Una recta queda determinada por un <stro: A line is settled by a point $P(p_1,p_2)$ it passes through and a direction vector $\vec{v}=(v_1,v_2)$ marking its direction. With that, any point of the line is reached by going from $P$ a multiple of $\vec{v}$.

It reads: “the point x, y equals the point p one, p two plus t times the vector v one, v two, with t in the reals”.

How to think of it: $(p_1,p_2)$ is where you start and $\vec{v}$ is which way you go. The $t$ is how far you go: with $t=0$ you are at the starting point, with $t=1$ you have covered the whole vector, and with $t$ negative you go backwards. That is why it is the form a robot uses: it says where it is at each instant.

Cinco formas para la misma recta no es u: Five forms for the same line is no whim: each answers a different question well. The explicit $y=mx+n$ is the one read at a glance on a graph of data; the parametric is the one a robot or a drone uses, because it describes where it is at each instant; the general one suits the computer for deciding which side of the line a point falls. Knowing how to change between them is knowing how to choose the tool.
La idea de describir una figura con una: The idea of describing a figure with an equation is Descartes', in 1637, and it appears in a hundred-page appendix to a philosophy book. It was possibly the most fertile unification in the history of mathematics: until then geometry and algebra were separate disciplines with different languages, and since then any problem in one can be translated into the other. That we call the axes Cartesian comes from that.

La distancia de un punto a una recta es: The distance from a point to a line is the length of the perpendicular segment joining them, which is the shortest path. With the general equation it comes from a direct formula:
d(P, r) = \\frac{|A p_1 + B p_2 + C|}{\\: d(P, r) = \frac{|A p_1 + B p_2 + C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}
Esta fórmula tiene una segunda vida fuer: This formula has a second life outside geometry. If the points are data of two classes and the line is the boundary separating them, this distance measures how much margin the boundary leaves, and choosing the line that makes it largest gives one of the classic classifiers. It is in [[ia-margen|the boundary with the widest margin]], where the denominator $\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ is exactly what has to be minimised.
